passages.title: Received wisdom must become patient speech and care for people in need
passages.summary: James, a servant of God, writes to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion. He tells them to count trials as joy, because testing produces endurance. Anyone who lacks wisdom should ask God, who gives generously. The rich will fade like a flower in the heat. God tempts no one; each is drawn by his own desire. Every good gift comes from the Father of lights. All should be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. Pure religion is to visit orphans and widows and stay unstained by the world.
passages.uncertainty: James names no place, so the map shows none. The city in chapter 4 is unnamed.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson applies asking for wisdom to Joseph Smith's experience. Why does the mirror example make hearing without action a form of self-deception?

contextNote.title: Received wisdom must become patient speech and care for people in need
contextNote.text: Verse 19 told the readers to be quick to hear. Verse 22 adds that hearing is not enough. One who only hears deceives himself. Verses 23–24 compare him to a man who sees his face in a mirror. He looks, goes away, and forgets what he was like. Verse 25 describes the doer, who looks into the law and continues. Verse 27 names what doing looks like: care for orphans and widows.

passages.title: Favoring wealth and withholding help expose a faith that remains only words
passages.summary: James tells the readers not to show favoritism. A man with a gold ring gets a seat, and a poor man stands. God chose the poor to be rich in faith. Favoritism breaks the royal law to love a neighbor as oneself. James then asks what good faith is without works. Even the demons believe that God is one, and they shudder. Abraham offered Isaac, and Rahab received the messengers. As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead.
passages.uncertainty: James names no place, so the map shows none. The city in chapter 4 is unnamed.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson joins active faith with love regardless of outward appearance. How does the unmet need for food test a spoken claim to faith?

contextNote.title: Favoring wealth and withholding help expose a faith that remains only words
contextNote.text: Verse 14 asks whether a faith with no works can save. Verses 15–16 answer with a case. A brother or sister lacks clothing and daily food. Someone wishes them peace, warmth, and food, and gives nothing. The words are kind, and the body still has nothing. Verse 16 asks what good that is. Verse 17 applies the case: faith by itself, without works, is dead.

passages.title: Small acts of speech require judgment that produces peace instead of rivalry
passages.summary: James warns that not many should become teachers, for they are judged more strictly. A bit turns a horse, and a small rudder turns a ship. The tongue is small and boasts great things. It is a fire that can set a forest ablaze. People tame animals, but no one can tame the tongue. The same mouth blesses God and curses people. James asks if a spring gives fresh and bitter water. Wisdom from above is pure, peaceful, gentle, and full of mercy.
passages.uncertainty: James names no place, so the map shows none. The city in chapter 4 is unnamed.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson teaches words that help people rather than cause harm. Why does blessing God conflict with cursing people made in God's image?

contextNote.title: Small acts of speech require judgment that produces peace instead of rivalry
contextNote.text: Verse 8 calls the tongue a restless evil. Verse 9 gives the evidence, and it comes from worship. With the tongue we bless our God and Father. With the same tongue we curse people. The verse says why the two cannot fit: people are made in God’s image. To curse the image while blessing the one it reflects is a contradiction. Verses 11–12 add that a spring does not give two kinds of water.

passages.title: Conflicting desires and confident plans must answer the limits of human control
passages.summary: James asks where their fights come from and answers: from their desires. They ask and do not receive, because they ask wrongly. Friendship with the world is enmity with God. God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble. They should draw near to God, and he will draw near to them. They should not speak against or judge one another. James then addresses those who plan a year of trade and profit. They do not know what tomorrow holds, for life is a vapor.
passages.uncertainty: James names no place, so the map shows none. The city in chapter 4 is unnamed.

lds.text: How does uncertainty about tomorrow challenge both boasting and delayed good work?

contextNote.title: Conflicting desires and confident plans must answer the limits of human control
contextNote.text: Verse 13 quotes merchants who plan a city, a year, trade, and gain. Verse 14 gives two facts against the plan. They do not know tomorrow, and their life is a vapor. Verse 15 does not forbid planning. It gives the sentence they should say first: “If the Lord wills.” Even living is put under that condition, before “do this or that.” Verse 16 names the fault in the first speech: it was boasting.

passages.title: Unpaid wages and shared prayer place endurance within care for wronged and vulnerable people
passages.summary: James tells the rich to weep, for their wealth has rotted. The wages they kept back from their field workers cry out. They have lived in luxury and condemned the righteous. The brothers are to be patient, like a farmer waiting for rain. They should remember the prophets and the endurance of Job. They should not swear, but let their yes be yes. The sick should call the elders to pray and anoint with oil. Elijah prayed, and one who turns a sinner back saves a soul.
passages.uncertainty: James names no place, so the map shows none. The city in chapter 4 is unnamed.

lds.text: The selected Church lesson joins patient endurance with fair treatment of others. How do withheld wages and shared prayer make endurance include care for other people?

contextNote.title: Unpaid wages and shared prayer place endurance within care for wronged and vulnerable people
contextNote.text: Verses 1–3 warn the rich that their stored wealth will witness against them. Verse 4 names one source of that wealth. Laborers mowed their fields, and the pay was kept back by fraud. Two things cry out: the wages and the reapers. The cries reach “the Lord of Armies,” a title of power. Verse 6 adds that the righteous one does not resist them. Verse 7 then tells the brothers to be patient until the Lord comes.
